extracted.intended_audience: students or readers learning elementary algebra (binomial/multinomial multiplication and division); historical/antique-mathematics readers
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural rules and didactic prescriptions for multiplying binomials/multinomials, raising them to powers, and dividing by binomials using row/column arrangements, reciprocals, and geometric (line-square) analogies. The page gives step-by-step operations, examples and conventions for arranging intermediate products and collecting like terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiply binomials by cross-multiplication
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiply each term of one binomial by each term of the other (cross or 'incroci') and place the resulting products in appropriate rows/positions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The page repeatedly instructs to 'multiplica ... incroci' — i.e. multiply terms pairwise (a×c, a×d, b×c, b×d), arrange these products in rows, then combine like-degree terms. Examples show placing successive products in the same line or successive lines so they can be summed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arrange intermediate products in rows and sum columns
rubrics_metrics.description: When performing multiplications, write each set of partial products in lines (rows) so that like-place/like-degree terms line up vertically and can be added.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text repeatedly uses the method of placing every multiplication 'in una riga' and then summing ('recale tutte pirma a una riga', 'poi metti tutte in vna riga'). This alignment/column-sum convention is central to obtaining final coefficients.

rubrics_metrics.name: Repeated multiplication to obtain powers (higher exponents)
rubrics_metrics.description: To compute squares, cubes, and higher powers of a binomial, multiply repeatedly by the binomial, using the previously obtained product as a factor for the next multiplication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples show computing square, cube, etc., by successive multiplications (e.g., get square by multiplying the binomial by itself, then multiply the result again for the cube), and organizing intermediate results in rows as above.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use squares, doubles, triples relationships
rubrics_metrics.description: Relate the square of a binomial to the squares of its individual terms and twice the product of the terms; analogously use triple/double relations when relevant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text states that the square of the binomial equals the square of the first term plus the square of the second plus twice the product; similarly, references to 'triplo', 'duplo', and differences of squares guide shortcuts and checks during multiplication and power-raising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiply multinomials by expanding each term across
rubrics_metrics.description: For trinomials, quadrinomials and general multinomials, multiply each term of one polynomial across every term of the other, treating the operation like repeated binomial multiplications and then collect like terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author prescribes treating each term successively (e.g., 'ogni multinomio' and 'metti tutte altre meatioi ... copolle') and shows examples of producing many rows of products to be combined into the final polynomial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect like terms and simplify final polynomial
rubrics_metrics.description: After computing and aligning partial products, combine terms of the same degree (same 'ordine' / like-name) and sum their coefficients to yield the final simplified polynomial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Multiple passages emphasize that after all multiplications are written the similar (simili) terms must be collected and added ('tutte le simili ... farai'). The final step is to reduce to the simplest form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplication using place-value shifts (alignment for powers of base)
rubrics_metrics.description: When multiplicands involve powers (e.g., powers of 10 or repeated factors like 102, 400, etc.), shift/align rows according to place-value (baffo/position) before summing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text contains many numeric examples where multiplications by large powers produce rows shifted ('piu baffo') and shows that correct placement of partial products (shifting by position) is necessary for correct summation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division by binomials via reciprocal/partition technique
rubrics_metrics.description: Divide a polynomial by a binomial by finding appropriate partitions/parts (reciprocals) of the dividend that match multiples of the divisor, subtracting successive products to reduce the remainder.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author repeatedly explains division as producing a 'recifo' (reciprocal/quotient) for the binomial and obtaining it by partitioning the dividend into parts that correspond to the binomial's terms, then performing successive multiplication/subtraction steps; geometric analogies to lines and squares are used in explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose a universal partition (data rule) for division
rubrics_metrics.description: Select an initial partition or placement ('Data regale' / 'Data regla') within the binomial/dividend that is general and valid for successive operations; this choice guides the subsequent division steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text insists the chosen 'data' must be universal and provable; once a sound starting partition is chosen the rest of the division proceeds systematically. Several paragraphs justify and exemplify this 'data' selection and its verification.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use geometric interpretation: terms as lines, products as rectangles, squares as areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpret algebraic quantities as geometric lines whose squares represent squared terms and whose rectangle-areas represent products; use these analogies to reason about multiplication and division.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author maps algebraic manipulations to geometry: 'lo quadrato de la linea a b' etc., and uses the equality of areas and squares to motivate and check algebraic rules (e.g., that the square of a sum equals sum of squares plus twice the rectangle).

rubrics_metrics.name: Divide by decomposing the dividend into parts corresponding to divisor factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Partition the dividend into parts so that each part corresponds to a factor (or multiple) of the divisor; then determine quotient parts so their product with the divisor reconstructs the dividend.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many examples show splitting the dividend into specified parts (e.g., by factors of 2,4,6, etc.), using these parts to obtain terms of the quotient; the method includes verifying by re-multiplication that the constructed product equals the original dividend.

rubrics_metrics.name: When multiplying/dividing, respect proportional relationships of coefficients
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep track of proportional relationships among coefficients (duplo, triplo, partie) so that when partitioning or reconstructing products/quotients the proportional scaling is preserved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explains how multiples (double/triple etc.) of terms of the binomial or quotient affect resulting products, and prescribes partitioning so that proportionalities remain coherent (e.g., dividing a product into halves/quarters to produce expected multiples).
